title: Cap what agent memory retrieves and the knowledge graph drops from first to last
summary: The PAIM scientific-memory benchmark found Graphiti's convincing win over plain chunk retrieval reversed once retrieval budget was controlled.
takeaways: Score every agent memory system at a fixed retrieval budget before you believe its leaderboard win.
Graph memory's reported gains can come from pulling far more text into the window — tokens you pay for, latency you wait on, and context the task no longer gets.
Control the budget and re-score; on one benchmark the graph output went from first at 8.04 to last at 5.27, behind a plain chunk baseline's 7.25.
sourceName: arXiv — Beyond Memory Leaderboards: Evaluating Scientific Memory as Budgeted Context Restoration (Sheverev, Finkelstein, Nikolenko)

body:
## What happened

A scientific-memory benchmark posted on 18 July 2026 evaluated eight memory systems over full papers: [on PAIM Graphiti wins convincingly but uses 2.6M characters of retrieved context per query, and after controlling for retrieval budget the lead disappears](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16848). At the fair-comparison anchor the graph's KG-only output scored 5.27 — [last of the six systems that could be budgeted](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.16848v1), two points behind the plain chunk retrieval it had beaten 8.04 to 7.22. A [controlled four-way ablation published the same day](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16604) landed in the same place: "knowledge-graph augmentation provides no reliable accuracy improvement across generators or question types in this corpus."

## Why it matters

If you pick agent memory on benchmark scores, you may be buying a context subsidy and calling it an architecture. Retrieved volumes across these systems ["differ by more than two orders of magnitude, so any comparison that does not control for them is comparing budgets as much as architectures"](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.16848v1).

## How it works

1. **Native scores are unbudgeted.** Each system retrieves as much as it likes, so the gap between them confounds structure with sheer volume.
2. **Fix characters-per-query, then re-score.** Even under the cap the graph pulled ~59K characters per query against the baseline's ~31K, and still lost.
3. **Spend the budget on retrieval quality before structure.** On the second corpus a sparse-dense hybrid was "the single most significant intervention" — at 50K the [hybrid variants of Simple RAG, Mem0, and Theoria tied within 0.03 points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16848).

> Judge a memory system by what it recalls per token of context it spends.

## The catch

Theoria is the authors' own system, so the load-bearing number is the chunk baseline they did not build. The finding is also scoped to single-shot retrieval over a fixed corpus. A separate instrument posted [24 July 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21962) found rankings invert with tenure: by nine weeks a provenance-typed graph reached 90.4% recall while the budgeted curated map fell to 78.4% — though that paper's best backend is its own author's layered system at 93.2%. Graphs may still earn their build cost in memory that accumulates for months.
